verdict.headline: Follower sustained sub-3s clearance for 5.7 of 6.9s while lead braked repeatedly; clearance hit 0.0s at segment end.

applicable_rules.reason: Follower (car) maintains a tracked gap behind a lead car on a motorway; clearance_s and gap_s both fall persistently below the 3-second sufficiency calibration for good (dry, overcast) conditions, and drop to zero as the lead brakes repeatedly.
applicable_rules.text: A driver must drive a sufficient distance behind a vehicle travelling in front of the driver so the driver can, if necessary, stop safely to avoid a collision with the vehicle.

evidence_assessment.summary: Both governing metrics (clearance_s, the stricter clear-road measure) and the bumper-to-bumper gap_s converge: sustained time below the 3s threshold is 5.7 of the 6.9s segment (~83%), well past the 5s transiency cutoff. The segment ends with a cluster of 10 lead_brake events and a final sample showing clearance_s = 0.0 (gap_m 4.28m vs follower length 4.6m), indicating the follower had essentially no clear road ahead to stop in.

key_statistics.interpretation: Average clear-road time well under the 3s good-conditions threshold, indicating general insufficiency, not just a momentary dip.
Exceeds the 5s sustained threshold in the transiency doctrine; strongly supports a Rule 126 breach rather than a transient dip.
Identical value under the alternative rear-to-rear convention; the two measurement conventions converge on the same sustained-breach conclusion.
Meets the >=3s sustained-below-2s threshold, an independent aggravating sustained-closeness signal.
During active closing (seconds_closing=2.99s) collision would occur in 1.34s if speeds held - a dynamic hazard signal.
At t=6.9s the clear road between vehicles is effectively zero; under the clearance_s convention this is a stopping-distance failure.

sample_citations.claim: gap_s dips to 1.99s and clearance_s to 1.56s as lead begins braking sequence.
ttc_s falls to 3.60s with v_rel +18.6 km/h (follower closing) while lead decelerates sharply (lead_speed 12.25 km/h).
clearance_s 1.21s, gap_s 1.76s, both well under 3s threshold, during continued lead braking.
clearance_s reaches 0.0 (gap_m 4.28m vs follower length 4.6m), gap_s 0.42s - critical insufficiency at segment end.

event_citations.legal_significance: Lead decelerates 17.4 km/h while follower clearance is already sub-2s (sample t=5.75 clearance_s=1.81), showing follower had no buffer to absorb lead's braking.

Final in a cluster of 10 braking events immediately preceding the near-zero clearance sample at t=6.9, evidencing the follower's distance was insufficient to safely react to a braking lead vehicle - the precise harm Rule 126 targets.

perception_caveats: Speeds are vision-tracked (not speedometer-derived) and carry a few km/h of noise; follower speeds here range ~5-40 km/h, so relative/closing-speed-derived TTC values carry compounded uncertainty.

13 of 96 samples (13.5%) were excluded for low confidence (none excluded for out-of-range, all within the 120m reliable range and calibration RMSE is very low at 0.018m), so the sustained-duration statistics are based on 83 usable samples and may slightly over- or under-state true sustained time.
gap_s_uncertainty_estimate is very small (0.002s), suggesting high internal consistency of the distance/speed pipeline, but this does not capture systematic vision-tracking speed bias.
Segment duration is only 6.9s - short enough that 'sustained' findings rest on a limited window, though the 5.7s sustained-below-3s figure spans the great majority of it.

reasoning_chain.claim: Rule 126 is engaged because the follower is tracked travelling behind a lead vehicle on a motorway and must maintain distance sufficient to stop safely.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Rule 126 applies to any driver following another vehicle, irrespective of vehicle class.

reasoning_chain.claim: Conditions are good (dry, overcast, sealed motorway), so the 3-second calibration applies rather than the 4+/5+ second poor-condition or heavy-vehicle standards.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: NSW sufficiency calibration: 3 seconds in good conditions.

reasoning_chain.claim: clearance_s (the stricter, clear-road measure) is treated as the governing test per the measurement convention; mean_clearance_s=1.857s and median=1.713s are both well under 3s.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Clearance_s better represents the road space available to stop, the substance of the Rule 126 test.

reasoning_chain.claim: sustained_clearance_below_3s_seconds = 5.7s exceeds the >=5s sustained threshold for good conditions, defeating the transiency doctrine (which would excuse dips under 5s).
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Transiency doctrine: sustained_below_3s_seconds >= 5s in good conditions strongly supports a Rule 126 breach.

reasoning_chain.claim: The rear-to-rear gap_s convention produces an identical sustained_below_3s_seconds value (5.7s), so the breach finding does not depend on which convention is preferred - both converge.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Where both clearance_s and gap_s agree, uncertainty about measurement convention does not change the verdict.

reasoning_chain.claim: A cluster of 10 lead_brake events between t=3.65s and t=6.35s, concurrent with clearance_s and gap_s already sub-2s, culminates in clearance_s=0.0 at t=6.9s - demonstrating the follower lacked sufficient buffer to respond safely to the lead's deceleration.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Rule 126's core concern - ability to stop safely if the lead brakes - is directly evidenced by this sequence.

reasoning_chain.claim: min_ttc_s=1.34s during an active closing phase (seconds_closing=2.99s) is an aggravating dynamic-hazard signal, though sustained_ttc_below_3s_seconds is brief (0.15s), limiting escalation to dangerous/negligent driving territory.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Falling TTC while closing aggravates a Rule 126 case but a single brief low-TTC moment alone does not establish dangerous driving.

reasoning_chain.claim: Rule 127 is not engaged because the follower (4.6m) is not a 'long vehicle' (>7.5m); the lead vehicle's length is irrelevant to Rule 127 applicability.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Rule 127 applies only when the following vehicle itself is a long vehicle outside a built-up area.

aggravating_factors.factor: Sustained sub-3s clearance for 5.7 of 6.9 seconds (~83% of segment) in good conditions.
Clearance degraded to 0.0s and gap_s to 0.42s at the final sample, coincident with repeated lead braking.
Cluster of 10 lead_brake events in the final ~2.7s of the segment without the follower regaining a safe buffer.
min_ttc_s of 1.34s during an active closing phase.

mitigating_factors.factor: Segment is short (6.9s) with some early samples showing large safe clearance (e.g., t=0.65s, clearance_s=9.35s), suggesting the close-following behaviour developed during the segment rather than being constant throughout.
13 of 96 samples excluded for low confidence, introducing some uncertainty into the precise sustained-duration figures.
Speeds are vision-tracked with inherent noise, so TTC and closing-speed-derived aggravating factors carry additional uncertainty.

escalation_charges_to_consider: Negligent driving (s117 Road Transport Act 2013 (NSW)) - only if further evidence confirms the near-zero clearance at t=6.9s was not a brief perception artifact

verdict.counterfactual: If the final low-clearance sample (t=6.9s, clearance_s=0.0) were discounted as a momentary tracking artifact and sustained_clearance_below_3s_seconds fell under the 5s transiency threshold, the verdict would likely downgrade to possible_breach.
verdict.explanation_for_lay_user: The camera data shows the following car staying closer than the recommended 3-second safety gap for most of the clip (about 5.7 out of 6.9 seconds), and this holds true whether you measure gap from bumper-to-bumper or the actual clear road between the cars. Near the end, the lead car braked ten times in quick succession, and by the final moment the gap had shrunk to almost nothing (0 seconds of clear road), which is exactly the kind of situation Rule 126 is meant to prevent. There's some uncertainty because vehicle speeds come from video tracking rather than a speedometer, and a few data points were dropped for low confidence, but the overall pattern strongly points to a breach of the safe-following-distance rule.

verdict.headline: Follower closed from 4.4s to 0s clearance in 3.9s on wet motorway; TTC fell to 0.43s.

applicable_rules.reason: Follower (car, 4.6 m) progressively closed on lead vehicle on a wet motorway, with clearance_s and gap_s both falling well below the sufficiency-to-stop calibration for almost the entire observed segment, culminating in near-zero clearance and TTC of 0.43 s.
applicable_rules.text: A driver must drive a sufficient distance behind a vehicle travelling in front of the driver so the driver can, if necessary, stop safely to avoid a collision with the vehicle.

evidence_assessment.summary: Across the 3.9 s segment the follower accelerated from ~20 km/h to ~58 km/h while closing on a lead vehicle that was accelerating more slowly, driving clearance_s from 4.42 s down to 0.0 s and gap_s from 5.23 s down to 0.26 s. The road surface is wet (poor-condition threshold of 4+ s applies), and sustained_clearance_below_3s_seconds (3.65 s of the 3.9 s segment) shows the vehicle spent almost the entire window under even the lenient dry-condition 3 s benchmark.

key_statistics.interpretation: Nearly the entire 3.9 s segment had clear-road time below the dry-condition 3 s sufficiency benchmark; on wet road the applicable 4+ s benchmark is breached essentially throughout.
Exceeds the 3 s transiency-doctrine threshold's spirit for a 2 s cutoff, indicating sustained, not momentary, close following.
A time-to-collision this low, while actively closing, is a strong dynamic hazard signal consistent with imminent-collision risk absent driver correction.
The follower was closing on the lead for the entire observed duration with no recovery, ruling out a brief, self-correcting dip.
Mean clear-road time is well under both the 3 s (dry) and 4 s (wet) sufficiency calibrations.
Even under the less-stringent rear-to-rear gap_s convention (which includes the follower's own body length), the mean is still below the applicable wet-road 4 s threshold.
Confirms the breach persists under the alternative gap_s convention, reducing sensitivity of the verdict to the clearance_s vs gap_s choice.

sample_citations.claim: Segment begins with an adequate clearance_s of 4.42 s, i.e. compliant at the outset.
By mid-segment clearance_s has fallen to 1.51 s, already well below even the dry 3 s benchmark.
clearance_s = 0.37 s and ttc_s = 1.41 s, indicating critical closeness and active closing.
clearance_s = 0.0 s and ttc_s = 0.43 s at segment end, consistent with near-collision proximity and no safe stopping margin.

perception_caveats: Speeds are vision-tracked estimates (follower reaching up to 58.5 km/h) and carry a few km/h of noise; this affects derived gap_s/clearance_s/ttc_s precision at the margins.

1 of 79 samples was excluded for low confidence; 78 usable samples remain, which is adequate but the segment itself is short (3.9 s), limiting ability to assess whether this pattern persisted beyond the camera's field of view.
gap_s_uncertainty_estimate is reported as very low (0.002 s) reflecting homography precision, but this does not capture vision-speed estimation noise, which is the larger source of uncertainty.
No distances were dropped for exceeding max_reliable_range_m (120 m); all gaps observed (4.27-29.75 m) were well within reliable range.
Road surface recorded as wet while weather is dry_clear - this discrepancy is noted; the wet-surface figure is used as the governing (stricter) condition per the stated environment fields.

reasoning_chain.claim: Follower vehicle length (4.6 m) does not exceed 7.5 m, so Rule 127 (long-vehicle minimum distance) is not engaged regardless of lead vehicle length or road class.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Rule 127 applies only when the following vehicle itself is a long vehicle (>7.5 m).

reasoning_chain.claim: The governing test is clearance_s (clear road ahead), which fell from 4.42 s to 0.0 s across the segment, with sustained_clearance_below_3s_seconds = 3.65 s of the 3.9 s duration.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Rule 126 requires sufficient distance to stop safely; clearance_s is the stricter and more legally apt reading of 'distance behind' since it excludes the follower's own body length.

reasoning_chain.claim: Road surface is wet, triggering the poor-conditions calibration of 4+ seconds; mean_clearance_s (1.447 s) and median_clearance_s (1.52 s) fall far short of this benchmark for nearly the whole segment.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: NSW sufficiency calibration prescribes 4+ seconds in poor conditions (wet road).

reasoning_chain.claim: Under the alternative gap_s convention the verdict does not flip: sustained_below_3s_seconds (gap_s) = 3.3 s and mean_gap_s = 1.934 s, both still below the applicable wet-condition threshold.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Where both metrics converge on breach, the choice of convention does not materially affect the verdict, though it is disclosed per measurement-convention policy.

reasoning_chain.claim: The pattern is a sustained, continuous closing (seconds_closing = 3.9, the entire segment) rather than a brief post-cut-in dip, ruling out the transiency doctrine's exception.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Transiency doctrine excuses brief dips (<5 s); here the sub-3s condition persisted for 3.65 s of a 3.9 s window with no recovery, which is sustained behaviour supporting breach.

reasoning_chain.claim: min_ttc_s = 0.43 s at segment end is a strong aggravating dynamic signal of active, worsening closure rather than steady-state close-following.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: A falling/low TTC while closing is treated as an aggravating factor under the stated escalation framework.

aggravating_factors.factor: Continuous, unrecovered closing throughout the entire 3.9 s segment with no stabilization.
min_ttc_s of 0.43 s indicates near-collision dynamics at segment end.
Wet road surface increases required stopping distance/time, making the observed sub-2s clearance more dangerous than the same figures would be in dry conditions.
Location is a Safe-T-Cam enforcement zone, relevant to penalty-notice amount for heavy vehicles (not applicable here, both cars) but indicates active enforcement context.

mitigating_factors.factor: Segment is short (3.9 s); the full before/after context of the maneuver (e.g., possible lead braking or lane change) is not captured.
Segment begins with a compliant clearance_s of 4.42 s, suggesting the follower was initially driving safely before the closing behaviour began.
No horn, high-beam, or other menacing-behaviour events recorded, reducing (but not eliminating) support for predatory-driving escalation.

escalation_charges_to_consider: dangerous driving (s52A Crimes Act 1900 (NSW)) if independently corroborated by additional evidence of risk to others

verdict.counterfactual: If the follower's speed had tracked the lead's acceleration (instead of outpacing it), keeping clearance_s above ~3-4 s throughout, this would be an unlikely_breach rather than a likely_breach.
verdict.explanation_for_lay_user: The camera tracked a following car that kept accelerating faster than the car ahead on a wet motorway, shrinking the clear road space between them from over 4 seconds down to essentially zero by the end of the clip. Even allowing for the fact that vehicle speeds are camera-estimated and carry some noise, this pattern persisted for almost the entire 3.9-second clip, not just a brief moment, and the time-to-collision dropped to under half a second near the end. This strongly suggests the follower was not leaving enough distance to stop safely, which is what NSW Rule 126 requires; the heavy-vehicle Rule 127 does not apply here since neither car is a long vehicle.

verdict.headline: Car sustained ~1.3-1.5s clearance behind articulated truck in heavy rain, far below the 4s wet-weather threshold.

applicable_rules.reason: Follower (car) maintained a gap behind a lead vehicle on a wet motorway that, per clearance_s and gap_s aggregates, was insufficient to stop safely for almost the entire 3.7s observed segment.
applicable_rules.text: A driver must drive a sufficient distance behind a vehicle travelling in front of the driver so the driver can, if necessary, stop safely to avoid a collision with the vehicle.

evidence_assessment.summary: Across 55 usable samples, clearance_s (the stricter, body-length-corrected measure) averaged 1.537s and never exceeded ~2.1s, while sustained_clearance_below_3s_seconds (3.65s) covers essentially the entire 3.7s segment. Under rain_heavy/wet conditions the applicable sufficiency threshold is 4+ seconds, which both clearance_s and gap_s fail almost continuously, and a dynamic closing event (min_ttc_s=2.14 at t=3.1) coincides with a cluster of hard lead-vehicle braking events.

key_statistics.interpretation: Well under even the 3s 'good conditions' baseline, let alone the 4s wet-weather threshold.
Worst-case clear-road time is less than half the required wet-weather margin.
Near-entirety of the 3.7s segment was spent below the 3s threshold on the stricter clearance measure, defeating the transiency doctrine.
Using the less-strict gap_s convention, almost the whole segment also fails the wet-weather 4s standard.
A brief but real dynamic collision-risk window during active closing, occurring amid repeated lead braking.
Follower was closing on the lead for the majority of the segment, consistent with insufficient following distance rather than steady-state gap-holding.

sample_citations.claim: Earliest sample already shows clearance_s=1.363, below both 3s and 4s thresholds from the start of the window.
clearance_s drops to 1.317 (segment minimum) coinciding with an 18.5 km/h lead_brake event.
ttc_s falls to 2.14s while lead speed collapses to 2.17 km/h, the closest approach to a dynamic collision risk in the segment.
Final sample shows partial recovery (clearance_s=2.111, gap_s=2.984), suggesting the follower was beginning to open the gap as the segment ends.

event_citations.legal_significance: 18.5 km/h speed drop while follower clearance was already at its minimum (1.317s), sharply reducing available reaction margin.
Coincides with min_ttc_s=2.14, the most acute dynamic hazard point in the segment.
Shows the follower was reactively managing the gap from the very start, indicating awareness of insufficient margin rather than inattention.

perception_caveats: Speeds are vision-tracked estimates, not speedometer-derived; expect several km/h of noise, which propagates into gap_s/clearance_s/ttc_s.
Segment duration is only 3.7s - a short window; sustained_* statistics describe this window only and cannot confirm a longer-term pattern beyond it.
1 of 56 samples excluded for low confidence; 0 excluded for out-of-range (within the 120m reliable limit), so range is not a material limitation here.
gap_s_uncertainty_estimate is very small (0.002s), indicating high internal consistency of the homography-derived distances, but this does not remove vision-speed noise.
Multiple overlapping lead_brake events make it difficult to fully separate lead-vehicle erratic braking behaviour from follower following-distance choice.

reasoning_chain.claim: Rule 127 is not engaged because the FOLLOWER (car, 4.6m) is not a long vehicle (>7.5m); the lead truck's length (16m) is irrelevant to triggering Rule 127.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Rule 127 applies only when the following vehicle itself is a long vehicle outside a built-up area.

reasoning_chain.claim: Conditions are wet/rain_heavy, raising the applicable sufficiency calibration from 3s to 4+ seconds.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: NSW sufficiency calibration requires 4+ seconds in poor conditions (wet, night, fog).

reasoning_chain.claim: Clearance_s (the stricter, legally preferable reading of the clear-road test) averaged 1.537s and was below 3s for 3.65 of 3.7s - i.e., almost the entire observed segment - well short of the 4s wet threshold.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Sustained sub-threshold following (not a brief dip) supports a Rule 126 breach under the transiency doctrine.

reasoning_chain.claim: Gap_s (the less strict, bumper-inclusive measure) also fails the 4s wet threshold for 3.65 of 3.7s, so the measurement-convention choice does not change the overall verdict, only the severity margin.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Both candidate interpretations of the '2/3-second rule' point to the same breach conclusion here.

reasoning_chain.claim: A dynamic closing event (min_ttc_s=2.14 at t=3.1) coincided with repeated hard lead braking (events at t=2.8-3.55), showing the follower was exposed to an active, not merely static, collision risk.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Falling/low TTC while closing is an aggravating dynamic signal under the stated framework.

reasoning_chain.claim: sustained_ttc_below_3s_seconds=0.0 indicates the dangerous TTC dip was brief/isolated rather than continuously sustained, moderating (but not eliminating) the dynamic-hazard aggravation.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Isolated dynamic spikes are weighted less heavily than sustained static closeness, per the transiency doctrine.

aggravating_factors.factor: Wet/rain_heavy conditions demand a higher 4s threshold, which was violated almost continuously.
Lead vehicle is a large articulated truck (16m) with a longer/heavier stopping profile, increasing the real-world risk of insufficient following distance.
Minimum TTC of 2.14s occurred during a cluster of hard lead braking events, indicating real dynamic risk, not just static proximity.
Site is flagged as a Safe-T-Cam enforcement zone, relevant to penalty tier consideration.

mitigating_factors.factor: Lead vehicle braked repeatedly and unpredictably (13 lead_brake events in 3.7s), suggesting erratic lead behaviour contributed to the closing dynamics, not solely follower choice.
Follower reacted with its own braking early in the segment (t=0.1), showing active gap management rather than inattention.
Segment is short (3.7s), limiting confidence that this reflects sustained long-duration behaviour rather than a difficult but brief traffic event.
By the final sample the follower appears to be increasing clearance (clearance_s rising to 2.111 at t=3.6), suggesting corrective behaviour.

verdict.counterfactual: If the low-clearance readings had been confined to a brief post-cut-in dip (<2s) rather than persisting for 3.65 of the 3.7s segment, the transiency doctrine would likely yield an unlikely_breach verdict instead.
verdict.explanation_for_lay_user: The camera data shows the car stayed only about 1.3-1.5 seconds of clear road behind a large truck for almost the entire 3.7-second clip, well short of the 4-second gap recommended in heavy rain. The truck also braked hard and repeatedly during this time, briefly bringing the collision-risk time-to-impact down to about 2 seconds. Because the car isn't a long vehicle, the special 60m long-vehicle rule doesn't apply, but the general 'leave enough room to stop safely' rule likely was breached. The short clip length and the truck's own erratic braking are noted as factors that add some uncertainty to how this would play out for a human reviewer.

verdict.headline: Clearance stayed under 2-3s for nearly whole segment; TTC fell to 1.52s during lead's hard braking, dawn/dusk lighting.

applicable_rules.reason: Follower car persistently close behind lead car on a motorway; both gap_s and clearance_s sit well under the sufficiency calibration for almost the entire 3.3s window, and TTC collapses during lead braking events.
applicable_rules.text: A driver must drive a sufficient distance behind a vehicle travelling in front of the driver so the driver can, if necessary, stop safely to avoid a collision with the vehicle.

evidence_assessment.summary: Both following-distance conventions show sustained sub-3s margins across effectively the whole 3.3s segment (sustained_clearance_below_3s_seconds=3.25, sustained_below_3s_seconds(gap)=3.25). Clearance_s, the stricter and governing metric, averages only 1.623s and bottoms at 0.893s at t=3.3, coinciding with repeated lead_brake events and a falling TTC (min 1.52s) during an active closing phase (seconds_closing=2.9s).

key_statistics.interpretation: Well below the 3s good-condition threshold and far below the 4s poor-condition (dawn/dusk) threshold.
At worst point, clear road ahead equates to under 1s reaction buffer - highly insufficient to stop safely.
Essentially the entire observed duration (3.3s) was below the 3s clearance threshold - not a brief dip.
Nearly half the segment also breached the stricter 2s clearance threshold.
Even the less strict rear-to-rear metric sits below the 3s good-condition calibration throughout most of the window.
During active closing, time-to-collision fell to 1.52s, an acute dynamic hazard coincident with lead braking.
Follower was closing the gap for ~88% of the segment, indicating insufficient buffer was being actively eroded, not merely static.

sample_citations.claim: Clearance_s already at 1.416s (sub-1.5s) before the most severe lead braking occurred, showing an already-insufficient buffer.
Clearance_s drops to 0.999s with ttc_s=1.537s immediately after a 23 km/h lead speed drop, a near-critical following distance.
Worst observed point: clearance_s=0.893s, gap_s=1.416s, well below both conventions' thresholds.

event_citations.legal_significance: 23 km/h deceleration by lead while follower's clearance was already under 1.5s - tests whether follower had sufficient buffer to stop safely, core Rule 126 question.
12.9 km/h deceleration contributing to the closing phase and falling TTC.
Early reactive braking by follower suggests awareness of closeness from the outset, partially mitigating culpability for initial positioning.

perception_caveats: Follower and lead speeds are vision-tracked estimates with a few km/h of noise; v_rel and TTC inherit this noise and should be read as indicative, not exact.
1 sample excluded for low confidence out of 67 total; no samples dropped for range (max_reliable_range_m=120m, well beyond observed gaps).

Segment duration is only 3.3s, which cannot satisfy the literal 'sustained_below_3s_seconds >= 5s' numeric threshold from the transiency doctrine even though the sub-threshold condition covers ~98% of the available window - this is a structural limitation of segment length, not evidence of a brief/transient dip.

Dawn/dusk lighting is treated here as a poor-condition factor (4+s calibration) despite the dry road surface; this interpretation affects severity but not the underlying breach finding since even the lenient 3s/gap_s convention is persistently breached.
gap_s_uncertainty_estimate (0.002s) reflects geometric/homography precision only and does not capture vision-speed estimation noise, which is the dominant uncertainty source for ttc_s and v_rel.

reasoning_chain.claim: Rule 126 is engaged because the vehicles are in a following relationship on a motorway and distance/speed data permit a sufficiency-to-stop analysis.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Rule 126 requires sufficient distance to stop safely to avoid collision.

reasoning_chain.claim: Clearance_s is adopted as the governing test per measurement convention; its mean (1.623s) and median (1.651s) are well under the 3s good-condition calibration.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Sufficiency calibration: 3s in good conditions.

reasoning_chain.claim: Dawn/dusk lighting arguably elevates the required margin to 4+ seconds; no sample in the segment reaches even the lower 3s bar, let alone 4s.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Sufficiency calibration: 4+ seconds in poor conditions.

reasoning_chain.claim: sustained_clearance_below_3s_seconds (3.25s) covers nearly the entire 3.3s segment, indicating persistent rather than transient insufficiency.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Transiency doctrine distinguishes brief dips (<5s) from sustained breaches.

reasoning_chain.claim: An active closing phase (2.9 of 3.3s) with min_ttc_s=1.52s coincided with escalating lead_brake events, showing the follower's margin was dynamically eroding exactly when the lead was decelerating hard.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Falling TTC while closing is an aggravating dynamic hazard signal under the stated framework.

reasoning_chain.claim: The less-strict gap_s convention tells a qualitatively similar story (mean 2.111s, sustained_below_3s_seconds=3.25s), so the choice of convention does not flip the verdict, only the margin of severity.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Both conventions must be disclosed per measurement convention requirement; divergence here is modest (~0.5s, consistent with follower_length_m/speed) and not verdict-changing.

reasoning_chain.claim: Segment brevity (3.3s) prevents literal satisfaction of the 5s sustained-threshold wording, introducing genuine uncertainty that justifies medium rather than high confidence.
reasoning_chain.legal_principle: Evidentiary sufficiency must be weighed against observation window limitations.

aggravating_factors.factor: Falling TTC to 1.52s coincident with a 23 km/h lead deceleration at a point of already-marginal clearance.
Dawn/dusk conditions should have prompted a larger buffer (4+s) than what was maintained (mean ~1.6-2.1s).
Near-total persistence of sub-3s clearance across the observed window rather than an isolated dip.

mitigating_factors.factor: Lead vehicle's own erratic, repeated hard braking (multiple lead_brake events) actively contributed to the shrinking gap, rather than the closeness being solely the product of follower's chosen distance.
Follower exhibited early reactive braking at t=0.1s, suggesting some situational awareness and responsiveness.
Short 3.3s segment limits certainty that the behaviour is 'sustained' in the full legal/doctrinal sense beyond the observed window.

escalation_charges_to_consider: Negligent driving (s117 Road Transport Act 2013 (NSW)) if corroborated by a longer observation window showing repeated near-critical TTC events

verdict.counterfactual: If the lead vehicle had not executed the escalating hard-braking sequence (especially the 23 km/h drop at t=2.75), clearance_s likely would have stabilised above 2s and the sustained-below-3s duration would shrink toward a transient dip, shifting the verdict toward possible_breach or unlikely_breach.
verdict.explanation_for_lay_user: The camera data shows the following car stayed closer than the recommended 2-3 second safety gap for almost the entire 3.3-second clip, using the stricter 'clear road ahead' measure. Things got worse near the end: the car in front braked hard several times, and the gap between the cars shrank so much that a collision could have happened in about 1.5 seconds if nothing changed. Because dawn/dusk lighting normally calls for an even bigger safety gap, and because this tight-following pattern covered almost the whole clip rather than being a brief one-off, this looks like a likely breach of the safe-following-distance rule, though the short clip length means we can't be fully certain this was a longer-term pattern.

verdict.headline: Wet-road following distance sustained near 2s clearance for ~5.2s, below the 4s wet-weather sufficiency benchmark.

applicable_rules.reason: Follower maintained a close, sustained gap behind lead car on a wet motorway for most of the 5.7s segment, engaging the 'sufficient distance to stop safely' test.
applicable_rules.text: A driver must drive a sufficient distance behind a vehicle travelling in front of the driver so the driver can, if necessary, stop safely to avoid a collision with the vehicle.
